explanation: Fires on the first sub-word piece of a word the tokenizer splits into several tokens, mostly lowercase word starts like ' br' (bricked, braced, brash, brachytherapy), ' l'(athered), ' ab'(ashed), ' fl'(anked), ' stri'(kers), and some name or identifier starts. What matters is the token being an incomplete word-initial fragment; whole words and function words give only weak activation.

No clear pattern. Fires on a mix of tokens: 'from' after 'arise'/'import {..}', digits inside years and numbers, transliteration contexts, 'as'/'of' in boilerplate legal or policy text, surname endings. It is hard to predict.

Fires mostly on function words ('is', 'of', 'as', 'in', 'at') that come right after a noun-phrase subject or head noun in the middle of a clause ('the difficulty is', 'the goal of', 'visible in searches'), plus assorted subword and code tokens. It is weakly specific.

Two jobs. (1) The '====' setext underline right after an 'Introduction' heading in arXiv-style markdown. (2) The first digit of a multi-digit number in a quantity, such as a CSS px value ('margin: 8px', 'padding: 10px'), a price, a score or a duration. Later digits and digits in years fire weakly.

Mixed. Fires strongly on 'Software' in 'Distributed under the Boost Software License', on the dots inside version numbers (TLSv1.2, 0.23.0, 1.0.2), and on type-annotation or syntax tokens in code and math (' :', ' ->', '}{'), plus some unrelated name fragments.

No coherent theme. Fires on random characters inside tokens/hashes, on prepositions after relational nouns or verbs ('member of', 'partnered with', 'in line with', 'between'), and on various code tokens.

Fires mainly on 'is' in a 'What is ...' question (dialogue, math problems, rhetorical questions), and on similar question continuations such as 'What on earth'. It also fires on some code punctuation tokens. The preceding 'What' is the key context.

Fires on tokens at the very start of boilerplate file headers and code: 'Copyright', '©', the year digit or 'The' after 'Copyright', 'License'/'@license', and 'function'/'void' after 'public'. It also fires moderately on question words ('How can', 'When is'). It is driven by the header or boilerplate context near the start of a file.
No clear theme. Fires on assorted subword continuations (cl-ank, cod-ility, cloud-front, St-uhlinger), 'msgstr' in .po files, 'Stack Overflow', and some phrase-internal words. Hard to predict.
Fires on tokens inside institution, organization or product names, especially acronym pieces (LE, CR, LLC, MAG, NIGMS, MKE) and 'of' in 'University of X'. Ordinary prose fires weakly.

Diffuse. Fires on a varied set: '[@' citation openers, 'What' starting a question, '...' spread syntax, '.biz'/'.Encoding', and assorted predicate words ('inspected', 'indispensable', 'unfit'). There is no single shared feature.

Fires on Go source-file boilerplate: 'build' in '// +build' constraint lines and 'import' right after a 'package' line (often after 'DO NOT EDIT' or license headers). It is weaker on 'package', 'github.com', 'vendor' and copyright years in Go/Kubernetes files. Both the token and the Go-file context matter.

Mixed. Fires on 'No' in 'U.S. Pat. No.', 'Scanner' in 'new Scanner(System.in)', pieces inside citation keys ([@ppat...], [@CR), 'opensource' in license URLs, and various other tokens. There is no unifying concept.

Fires on the word 'out', strongest in 'out of' ('4.2 out of 5 stars', 'out of phase', 'out of the water', 'arising out of'). It is weaker on other uses of 'out' (read out, outstripped, passed out) and on a few 'or'-initial fragments.

Fires mainly on forms of 'pose' (pose, poses, posing, posed), both the photo sense and the 'pose a risk/dilemma' sense, and on 'verse'. A second, unrelated job: pieces of uppercase acronyms (FSH, PFS, OSHA, SA, Pssh, vfs). It is weak elsewhere.

Diffuse. Fires on mid-word medical-term pieces (echoc-ardi-ography, arr-hythm-ias, ac-uity), words in copyright notices ('Group', 'Inc', 'granted'), the 'IRM' in 'AFFIRMED', years and numbers, and other mixed tokens.

Fires on 'more' in the patent formula 'relates to X and, more particularly, to Y' (strongest). It also fires on 'or'/'but'/'except' that open a hedging or alternative aside, often inside parentheses or after a list ('(or at least', ', or similar'). Ordinary prose 'more' or 'and' fires weakly.

Fires on scattered word-internal or word-final pieces (-hit, p5-3, FLOT-US, meditat-ion, RELIG-ION, Roose-velt), mostly in biomedical, legal or name contexts. There is no clear semantic common factor.

Fires on member-access and method-chaining tokens in code that join a preceding call, cast or object to the next method: ').', '().', '()->', '->', a leading '.' on a continuation line, '[record'. It is weaker on other code tokens such as 'int' and 'function'.

Fires on mid-word pieces of technical biomedical terms in abstracts (anticata-le-ptic, ret-ic-ulum, uter-ine, duoden-alis, intrac-avit-ary) and on tokens in legal captions and judge names, as well as config/code numeric tokens. It looks like a mix of technical-text continuation tokens.

Fires on words that refer jointly to two people or parties in a relationship or interaction (their, our, we, 'to' in 'met ... to', 'have been married', mutual, bilateral), especially romantic couples or two named partners. Pronouns outside a two-party relationship context fire weakly.
